processing: Stems and leaf veins sorted out while refining shaded gyokuro, blended with some leaf fragments and sold as a stem tea rather than discarded.
harvest_season: Follows the gyokuro harvest in spring; the stems are separated during refining.
appearance_dry: Pale green stem pieces mixed with darker fine needles of leaf.
appearance_wet: Light green soft stems among darker pieces of leaf.
taste_profile: Mild, gently sweet and rich in savouriness, with less bitterness than the leaf and a clean finish.

brewing.notes: Keep it cool, around 60–70°C: the leaf fragments in the mix turn bitter in hot water even though the stems would not.

vintage_note: Sold from the current year's crop like other Japanese greens, usually best within a year. It is priced below gyokuro from the same maker, and grades are named by the merchant, so compare within one seller's range.
description:
Gyokuro karigane is the stem tea of gyokuro: the fine stems and veins sorted out when the shaded leaf is refined, sold with some leaf bits mixed in. It is the classic way to get much of gyokuro's character for much less money.

Stem tea in general is called kukicha, and karigane is one name for it. Usage varies: some sellers keep the word for gyokuro stems only, others extend it to stems of good sencha. The word gyokuro on the packet settles that here. In Kyushu the same kind of tea is also called shiraore, and in Kyoto it is often just gyokuro kukicha.

In the cup it is soft, sweet and savoury, with relatively little caffeine because it is mostly stem. People often brew it too hot; about 65°C and a minute and a half is a good start, and the second steep should be quick.

Look for fine, fresh green stems and a clear statement of what they came from. This is a good everyday tea, and an easy first step toward full gyokuro.
history:
Little is documented about when karigane emerged as a named product. It belongs to the broader habit of selling stems sorted out during refining as a tea in their own right.

The name is written two ways, 雁ヶ音 and 雁金, and is usually read as referring to wild geese; sellers give differing explanations of why, and none is firmly established.
